lessons.title: Running the daily routine in a poultry house
lessons.html:
Why a fixed daily routine matters

Chickens are creatures of habit. Broilers, layers and breeders all perform best when feeding, lighting, egg collection and house checks happen at the same times every day. As the supervisor of a poultry unit, your job is to make sure that routine is planned, done properly and written down.

The first walk of the morning

Before anything else, walk every house slowly. Look, listen and smell. A healthy flock is evenly spread, active and calm. Warning signs include birds huddling (too cold), panting with wings held out (too hot), birds crowding at one end, a strong ammonia smell, wet litter, unusual sounds such as snicking or rattling breathing, and more dead birds than normal.

Core daily checks

  • Water: check drinkers or nipple lines work, the header tank is full and water is clean. Birds drink before they eat, so a water failure is an emergency.
  • Feed: check feeder lines run, pans are not empty or overflowing and the silo level is recorded.
  • Climate: read the thermometer and humidity readings, check fans, curtains, foggers and heaters, and compare with the breed management guide for the flock age.
  • Lighting: confirm the lighting programme and timers match the plan for that flock.
  • Mortality: remove, count and record dead birds by house and dispose of them by the farm's approved method.
  • Eggs (layers and breeders): collect at set times, record numbers, cracks and floor eggs.

Planning the day

After the walk, plan the work. Match people to tasks, for example one worker on egg collection and grading, one on mortality and litter, one on feed deliveries. Prioritise anything that affects bird welfare first: water, feed, temperature and sick birds. Maintenance and cleaning come after the birds are safe.

Keep a simple daily checklist for each house. A worker ticks each item and signs it. You check and countersign. This gives proof that the work was done and helps you spot patterns over time.

lessons.title: Supervising, recording and responding to problems
lessons.html:
Supervising the team during the day

Day-to-day management is not only about birds. It is about people, records and quick decisions. A good supervisor gives clear instructions at the start of the shift, checks work during the day and closes the day with a handover.

Giving instructions

Tell each worker what to do, in which house, by what time and to what standard. For example: Thabo, clean and refill the drinkers in House 3 before 10:00, then record the water meter reading. Check that the worker understood. New workers need to be shown, not only told.

Keeping daily records

Records turn observations into information. Each house should have a daily record sheet or app entry with:

  • date and flock age
  • mortality and culls
  • feed delivered and used
  • water meter reading
  • minimum and maximum temperature
  • egg numbers (layers) or sample weights (broilers)
  • treatments, vaccinations and visitors

A sudden drop in water use is often the first sign of disease, sometimes a day before feed intake or egg numbers drop. That is why water readings must be written down every day at the same time.

Responding to problems

When something is wrong, act in this order:

  1. Make the birds safe: restore water, feed, ventilation or power (start the generator if needed).
  2. Find the cause: blocked line, broken fan, tripped switch, or a health problem.
  3. Report: tell the farm manager straight away about any rise in mortality or sick birds. Suspected notifiable diseases such as avian influenza or Newcastle disease must be reported to the state veterinarian under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Do not move birds or people off the site until told.
  4. Record what happened and what you did.

End-of-day handover

Before you leave, do a last walk, check that the generator and alarm are ready and write a short handover for the night staff or the next shift.

Key points

  • Walk every house first thing and use your eyes, ears and nose.
  • Water, feed, climate and mortality are checked and recorded every day.
  • Bird welfare tasks come before cleaning and maintenance.
  • A drop in water use is an early warning sign of disease.
  • Report suspected notifiable diseases to the state vet immediately.
